title: This Projector Is So Well-Engineered, It Even Makes Bad Movies Look Good
gist: WIRED gives the AWOL Vision Aetherion Max RGB laser ultrashort throw projector a 9/10, praising its color accuracy (110% Rec. 2020), edge-to-edge clarity, daylight performance and 1ms gaming latency. At $4,499 list (discounted to $3,599 on Amazon) it competes with the Hisense XR10 and Xgimi Titan Noir Max, with minor flaws in auto-keystoning, height-channel audio and the remote.

themes.theme: Aetherion Max picture quality and brightness

insights.claim: WIRED's reviewer rated the AWOL Vision Aetherion Max RGB laser ultrashort throw projector 9/10, calling it a standout for color accuracy, edge-to-edge pixel clarity and contrast.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Strong reviews of premium home-cinema projectors signal competitive pressure on large-screen TV makers at the high end.
insights.quote: The AWOL Vision Aetherion Max is ultimately an amazing projector: a rock star of color accuracy, with crisp pixel clarity across the entire image and superior contrast.
insights.locator: The AWOL Vision Aetherion Max is ultimately

insights.claim: The Aetherion Max produced a watchable image in broad daylight on a nearly 16-foot diagonal wall, without noticeable contrast problems in nighttime scenes.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Daylight usability removes a key historical limitation of projectors versus TVs, widening the addressable market.
insights.quote: I didn't notice any contrast problems and could see nighttime scenes just fine.
insights.locator: The Aetherion Max's ability to work

insights.claim: AWOL Vision specifies the Aetherion Max at 110 percent of the Rec. 2020 color spec, a 6,000:1 contrast ratio and 3,300 ISO lumens, though the reviewer cautions such specs are not the final arbiter of picture quality.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Spec-sheet claims in consumer display hardware can diverge from real-world performance, so reviews matter for demand.
insights.locator: For color accuracy, the projector hits

insights.claim: The projector struggled on some demo-reel benchmarks: dark trees on dark backgrounds were hard to make out and skin-tone tests showed a lack of tonal variety that settings adjustments did not fix.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Remaining image-quality weaknesses show where premium projectors still trail rivals.
insights.quote: The skin-tone test also yielded unimpressive results.
insights.locator: The Aetherion Max also passed demo-reel

insights.claim: The Aetherion Max lists at $4,499 but was offered at $3,599 on Amazon, with AWOL's own listing at $4,999 discounted to $3,999, a price the reviewer says is in line with other high-end models.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Deep discounts from list price on premium projectors hint at pricing pressure in the high-end home-cinema segment.

insights.claim: At 19.3 pounds the Aetherion Max is notably lighter than the 23-pound Hisense XR10, and unlike the Xgimi Titan Noir Max its iris does not adjust dynamically during playback.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Feature-by-feature differentiation among AWOL Vision, Hisense and Xgimi defines the competitive map for premium UST projectors.
insights.quote: The portable projector weighs 19.3 pounds—notably less than its 23-pound competitor Hisense XR10 Smart Projector

insights.claim: The Aetherion Max runs Google TV, making setup take only a few minutes, and its remote includes a Google Gemini button and shortcuts for apps like Netflix.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Google's TV platform and Gemini assistant are being embedded in third-party premium hardware, extending its ecosystem reach.
insights.quote: This model runs on Google TV, and that’s a relief because it meant setup only took a few minutes.
insights.locator: This model runs on Google TV

insights.claim: The projector's 1-millisecond latency made it strong for gaming in tests with NBA 2K27 and Onimusha: Way of the Sword on an Alienware Aurora laptop with a new Nvidia GeForce driver.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Low-latency projectors broaden big-screen gaming use cases that benefit GPU and gaming-hardware demand.

insights.claim: The reviewer hit glitches: audio cut out with 7.1.2 height-channel speakers, phone-based QR keystone correction failed in a dark room, and the remote's volume buttons are small and not backlit; AWOL Vision is investigating the audio issue.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Software and QA rough edges can weigh on a premium brand's reputation against established competitors.
insights.quote: A slight glitch was that the audio cut out when I used height channel speakers for 7.1.2 sound (AWOL Vision is investigating why).
insights.locator: Sound is strong on the projector
